title: Приглашение в театр  (Invitation to the Theater)

segments.t: Arriving at work in the morning, Vika sees German holding a bouquet of flowers and assumes they are for her. German smoothly explains the flowers are for his sick aunt in the hospital and invites Vika to use the aunt's spare theater ticket that evening. Let's listen to their conversation in Russian.
Доброе утро, Герман, цветы не нужно.
Вы про цветы? Простите, это не вам.
Они для моей больной тёти.
Сходим сегодня вечером вместе в театр?
Я должен был пойти с тётей.
Но она вчера вдруг заболела.
Вы меня сегодня вечером выручите?
Хорошо, я с удовольствием пойду.
Запомни, мы встречаемся уже три года.
Ты сделал мне предложение руки.
Ты же просто моей подруге врёшь.
Мы выезжаем ровно в семь.
Let's break down German's theater invitation and Katya's rehearsal with Denis line by line.
Доброе утро, Герман, цветы не нужно.
'Good morning, German, flowers are not necessary.' Vika uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
Вы про цветы? Простите, это не вам.
'You mean the flowers? Forgive me, they are not for you.' German uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
Они для моей больной тёти.
'They are for my sick aunt.' German pairs 'crazy' with 'aunt' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
Сходим сегодня вечером вместе в театр?
'Shall we go to the theater together tonight?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and German's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.
Я должен был пойти с тётей.
'I was supposed to go with my aunt.' A masculine modal adjective with a past-tense auxiliary expresses an unfulfilled past plan.
Но она вчера вдруг заболела.
'But she suddenly fell ill yesterday.' An inceptive verb prefix marks the sudden onset of an illness in the past tense.
Вы меня сегодня вечером выручите?
'Will you help me out tonight?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and German's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.
Хорошо, я с удовольствием пойду.
'All right, I will go with pleasure.' Notice how Russian puts 'good, well, all right' and 'will go' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
Запомни, мы встречаемся уже три года.
'Remember, we have been dating for three years already.' Here Katya anchors the thought on 'to remember, to memorise' and finishes on 'years', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
Ты сделал мне предложение руки.
'You proposed marriage to me.' In everyday Russian, 'made' flows straight into 'hands' without extra linking words.
Ты же просто моей подруге врёшь.
'After all, you are just lying to my friend.' Katya pairs 'simply, just' with 'are lying' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
Мы выезжаем ровно в семь.
'We are heading out at seven sharp.' She sets the departure time using an adverb meaning sharp or exact and the numeral seven. Now let's hear the entire scene again without interruption.

Vika agrees to accompany German to the theater, while Katya tells Denis to be ready to leave at seven o'clock sharp. Notice how Russian expresses duration up to the present with a present-tense verb. See you next time!
До свидания!
